course.description:
This course introduces the full process of data science, from collecting raw data to building useful insights and models. Students will learn how to gather data from sources like websites and APIs, clean and prepare it for analysis, and label image or text data when needed. The course covers key steps in data science, including data wrangling, exploration, visualization, modeling, and evaluation.
In the image section, students will learn how to label and explore image data, apply clustering techniques like K-means to group visual patterns, and understand how to move from basic clustering to using pre-trained models for classification. For each method, students will learn how to evaluate performance using metrics such as accuracy and Intersection over Union (IoU).
In the text section, the course begins with text cleaning and basic techniques like TF-IDF. Students will then explore more powerful models like BERT, and learn how different models can be used for classification and language understanding tasks. Along the way, students will compare results using standard evaluation metrics.
Rather than focusing only on model training, this course emphasizes how to use data to answer real questions, communicate findings, and build end-to-end data science workflows. Students will use Python tools such as Pandas, Scikit-learn, Matplotlib, and Hugging Face Transformers to work on real datasets and complete hands-on projects.
This course is designed for students with basic Python and AI knowledge who want to deepen their understanding of the data science pipeline.
course.objectives: This course aims to help students understand the full process of data science, from collecting and preparing data to building and evaluating models. Students will learn how to handle different types of data, including text and images, and apply both basic and advanced techniques such as K-means clustering, TF-IDF, and classification. By the end of the course, students will be able to use Python tools to explore data, label datasets, apply machine learning models, and evaluate results using metrics like accuracy and IoU. They will also complete a small project to apply what they have learned in a real-world context.

course.description:
This course introduces students to the sociological study of technoscience and society. You will explore and analyze what it means to live in a contemporary technological society. A major goal will be to answer several questions: (1) What are the social, structural, and cultural influences on our behavior, attitudes, and technological change? (2) What are the sources, dynamics, and consequences of social inequality and of how we are organized? (3) What are the implications of materials and technology for social change? We will then discuss fundamental social processes and concepts—culture, organization and management, social identity, and social interaction.
In the later part of the semester, you will study how technology and society have been intertwined. While technology has always been an intricate part of any society, in the second half of the 20th-century technological change became a defining characteristic of the way societal structures, and technological politics are constituted and organized. In this part, you will investigate and unravel this distinctive condition. You will study different areas where questions about technology’s role in society are central: economy, transportation, and corporations. In this course, you will learn that technological development is not just about technology.

You will learn to recognize and apply analytical perspectives to analyze the entanglement of technology, media, and politics in our contemporary society.
You will be able to make a reasoned contribution to academic and societal debates on the role of technology in society.

course.description:
Recent advances in computing may place us at the threshold of a unique turning point in human history. Soon we are likely to entrust management of our environment, economy, security, infrastructure, food production, healthcare, and to a large degree even our personal activities, to artificially intelligent computer systems.
The prospect of "turning over the keys" to increasingly autonomous systems raises many complex and troubling questions. How will society respond as versatile robots and machine-learning systems displace an ever-expanding spectrum of blue- and white-collar workers? Will the benefits of this technological revolution be broadly distributed or accrue to a lucky few? How can we ensure that these systems respect our ethical principles when they make decisions at speeds and for rationales that exceed our ability to comprehend? What, if any, legal rights and responsibilities should we grant them? And should we regard them merely as sophisticated tools or as a newly emerging form of life?

course.description:
I. Course Objectives
This course is designed to help students understand the legal and governance issues arising from the development of digital technologies, with data governance as its central focus. It addresses major emerging topics, including personal data protection, artificial intelligence governance, digital platform accountability, open government data, data sharing, cybersecurity, cross-border data flows, and the European Union(EU)’s data governance framework.
Taught entirely in English, the course introduces students to core concepts in contemporary international technology law. It examines legal issues that arise throughout the data life cycle, from collection, processing, use, retention, and sharing to deletion. The course also considers the legality of artificial intelligence systems in model training and content generation, and analyzes the respective responsibilities and obligations of governments, businesses, digital platforms, and data intermediaries in data governance.
The course further incorporates Taiwan’s legal framework, the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Data Governance Act, Data Act, Artificial Intelligence Act, and other significant legislative developments and international trends. Through this comparative approach, students will develop a stronger interest in technology law and acquire the analytical skills needed to address practical legal issues.
II. Course Description
This course begins with legal issues related to data use as an entry point into technology law. It introduces key legal concepts, including personal data protection, informational self-determination, privacy, and data governance, before moving to issues such as open government data, data sharing, data intermediary services, data altruism, data access for Internet of Things devices and connected products, cloud switching, regulation of artificial intelligence technologies, algorithmic transparency, disclosure obligations, and legal requirements for cross-border data transfers.
The course focuses on recent developments in the EU’s data governance regime and explains how the GDPR, Data Governance Act, Data Act, and Artificial Intelligence Act together shape a technology law framework grounded in trustworthiness, data access, and risk management. In addition to introducing major international technology laws, the course includes weekly case discussions to help students examine the relationship between data governance, personal data protection, public interest, industrial innovation, digital market competition, national data sovereignty, and the protection of fundamental rights.
course.objectives:
Upon completion of this course, students will be able to:
Understand the foundational theories and regulatory structure of technology law and data governance.
Examine legal issues concerning personal data protection, data sharing, digital platform regulation, risk-based regulation of artificial intelligence, and cybersecurity safeguards.
Compare Taiwan’s digital legal framework with the GDPR, Data Governance Act, Data Act, and other major technology laws of the EU.
Assess, from legal and governance perspectives, personal data protection risks and appropriate levels of regulatory oversight arising from artificial intelligence and other technological applications.
Analyze current disputes and cases involving the application of technology law from an independent perspective and propose appropriate legal or policy reforms.

course.titleZh: 治理中國：政治變遷、社會轉型與台港澳關係
course.titleEn: Governing China: Political Change, Social Transformation, and Relation s with Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau
course.description:
This course examines the rise of China as the defining force shaping politics and society across the Greater China region. Over the past four decades, the People’s Republic of China (PRC) has transformed from a poor, isolated polity into the world’s second-largest economy and a leading geopolitical power — with profound consequences not only for its own governance but for its relationship with Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan, three societies bound to the mainland by deep cultural and historical ties yet possessing distinct institutional inheritances. The course asks: how has China’s rise reshaped the political institutions, social fabric, and external relationships of each of these polities, and what does the resulting variation tell us about the reach and the limits of Chinese-style governance?
The first half of the course maps the mainland system that drives these dynamics: major theoretical traditions for understanding Chinese politics (authoritarian resilience, fragmented and consultative authoritarianism, adaptive governance, party-state institutionalism); the organisation, ideology, and cadre system of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) under Xi Jinping; political change and policy implementation under the post-2012 leadership; the social transformation generated by urbanisation, hukou reform, demographic change, and growing inequality; and state–society relations including civil society, religion, ethnic politics, surveillance, and platform politics.
The second half traces how the rise of China has reshaped — and is being reshaped by — its peripheries. In Hong Kong, the asymmetric integration of the Special Administrative Region into the mainland’s political and economic order has accelerated since 2014, culminating in the 2020 National Security Law, the 2021 “patriots-only” electoral overhaul, and the 2024 Safeguarding National Security Ordinance (Article 23). In Macau, the rise of China has been managed through a quieter politics of accommodation, with deepening integration into the Greater Bay Area and continued reliance on a gaming economy increasingly aligned with Beijing’s strategic priorities. In Taiwan, China’s rise has driven both deepening economic interdependence (trade, investment, ECFA, semiconductors) and an intensifying security competition, with democratisation, identity politics, the 2024 presidential election, and the role of the United States all shaping the cross-Strait equation. The final two weeks are reserved for student case presentations.
course.objectives: By the end of the course, students should be able to: (1) compare leading theoretical models of Chinese governance and assess their analytical reach; (2) explain how the CCP organises power and recruits, monitors, and disciplines cadres; (3) trace the principal directions of political change under Xi Jinping; (4) analyse social transformation and state–society contention in mainland China; (5) compare the post-handover political trajectories of Hong Kong and Macau; (6) account for the trajectory of Taiwan’s democratisation and cross-Strait relations; and (7) deliver a research-grade case study and reflection note that engage critically with primary scholarship.

course.titleEn: Governing Environment by Numbers: the Practices and Politics of Sustai nability Metrics
course.description:
Course Description
This course has two aims. On one hand, It intends to help ICI (International College of Innovation) students acquire basic knowledge of sustainability reporting and carbon accounting. These are two popular tools in the corporate world of sustainability and in the field of environmental governance. On the other hand, this course also aims to equip ICI students with critical and historical perspective to understand the quantification logic behind the current trend of global environmental governance.
This course interweaves technical training and critical analysis throughout the semester: you will read sustainability reports learn the standards behind them, examine how metrics are constructed, and learn directly from practitioners’ insights. Specifically, this course collaborates NCCU's own Sustainability Office. We will use NCCU’s own Sustainability Report as a companion case and interact with the authors who craft the report from office. Furthermore, we will use the global higher education sector as our focus and collectively analyze how different universities develop their own Sustainability Reports and what the implications are.
Course Format
Class Activity & Group Discussion & Short Lecture:
I employ a
student-centered learning approach
in this course rather than a traditional lecture format (i.e., you listen to lectures to learn knowledge).
My role will be a facilitator who supports your learning. In particular, this course is built on group discussion and collective learning. Most learning will be based on reading assigned materials, discussion, and class activities. I will supplement these activities with short lectures that help contextualize readings, articulate learning themes across weeks, and move the discussion forward.
Learning Activities
Collective Annotation:
For most of the weeks, there is one assigned reading you need to finish reading before coming to the class. You will also be required to make 3 comments on a collective reading document. Your comments will be incorporated into the classroom activity and discussion.
Weekly online discussion
Each week, we are going to have TWO threads of discussion online. The platform we are going to use is
the LinkedIn private group
. The first thread is based on the weekly assigned reading and the collective annotation. The second thread is based on an existing LinkedIn post that is chosen by a designated student. You will be responsible to provide at least ONE response on each thread (meaning TWO responses in total). And you will also have a chance to share one LinkedIn post as our basis of discussion.
The design of this class activity also means each students need to create your own LinkedIn account. The goal is to help students get familiar with the platform and the content on the platform. LinkedIn is also an important source for the course topic – substantiality reporting, carbon accounting, and global environment management and governance.
While the use of LinkedIn in this course is a strategic choice intended to strengthen your learning, you should be mindful of a longer-term consequence of this design. Unlike a comment posted on a course platform that disappears when the semester ends, your contributions in this private LinkedIn group carry a "real stake": they are attached to the professional profile you will take with you into job-seeking, and they may persist beyond this course. This is deliberate. Part of the aim is for you to practice speaking thoughtfully in a professional setting where your name and your words are connected—which is also why participation should be a considered choice, not an afterthought. If you would prefer not to hold a LinkedIn account or not to post under your own name, you may want to avoid enrolling in this course.
Class participation and end-of-class exercise
It is critical to come to the class on time and participate in class activities. My assumption is that a fair proportion of your learning will come from your interaction and collaboration with your classmates during the class. Thus, it is imperative to attend every class except for legitimate reasons (e.g. sick leave or other types of leave permitted by the university).
Collaborative project – Surveying Sustainability Reporting in the Global Higher Education sector
Throughout the semester, our class will collectively produce a critical report on how higher education institutions around the world account for their environmental impacts. Working in groups, you will each analyze sustainability reports from universities in different countries, especially including reports written in languages other than English. We will examine the choices behind them: which frameworks they adopt, how they define what counts, what they measure, and what they leave out. Rather than scoring or ranking universities, our goal is to map the varieties of sustainability reporting practices in the higher education sector and to ask what these documents reveal about how universities understand their environmental responsibilities. More importantly, the goal is not to produce separate analysis by different students but to put together all the analysis as a coherent report. Ideally, we will publicly launch the initial draft of our collective report at the end of the semester. There will be different tasks throughout the semester to craft the report together. I will announce these tasks at the beginning of the semester.
Study Journal:
Study Journal is a Google document you share with me. I will provide detailed instructions later for how to create your Study Journal. I hope this Study Journal will serve as a platform for you to monitor and track your learning progress. It will also be a good way for me to know how you are doing during these four months and what measures I could do to support your learning. You will be responsible for maintaining this Study Journal throughout the 4-month course. In specific, this Study Journal will include four components.
At the beginning of the course, you will need to develop your learning schedule for all the course assignments stated in the syllabus. (mandatory)
In the 9
th
week of the course, you will need to do a mid-term reflection to evaluate your learning so far and how you may adjust your study plan in the next two months. (mandatory)
At the end of the course, you will need to write a brief report evaluating your learning during these four months. (mandatory)
You are welcome to write an update on your learning progress and status any time during the semester (e.g., once a week) on the same document. (optional)
course.objectives:

During this course, you will have the opportunity to learn how to:
Explain the rationale, structure, and major frameworks of sustainability reporting.
Describe the basic principles of carbon accounting.
Analyze how quantification logic shapes and constrains environmental governance.
Situate sustainability reporting and carbon accounting within their historical and political contexts.
Evaluate the limitations of quantification-based governance and propose alternative approaches.
Produce a collectively authored critical assessment of higher education sustainability reporting at the global scale.
Engage in a professional learning community by immersing in sustainability trends and discussing with peers on LinkedIn.

course.titleZh: 大型跨國調查資料之分析與應用
course.titleEn: Analysis and Application of Large-Scale International Survey Data
course.description:
Have you ever wondered if people in different countries really live differently? They often think differently about family, work, money, trust, happiness, and politics. They may also behave differently, follow different ways of life, and reach different results in education and health. For example, how many hours do people work, and are shorter working hours linked to more happiness? How do couples share housework across countries? How healthy do people stay as they grow older? And how well do students do in math and science in different school systems and education cultures? In this course, we use real survey data collected from people all around the world to study questions like these.
You will work with several famous international survey projects, including the World Values Survey (WVS), the East Asian Social Survey (EASS), the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP), the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), and the WHO Study on Global AGEing and Adult Health (SAGE).
This course gives you the tools to study that world with real evidence. Step by step, you will learn how these surveys are made, how to clean and prepare the data, how to compare answers fairly across countries, and how to turn your results into a clear report and a short presentation.
You do not need to be a “statistics person” to do well here. We start from the basics and build up slowly. Every new idea comes with a hands-on example, and we review the key statistics together in class before you need to use them. Class demonstrations use R (and Python templates will also be shared), but you may use any software you like for your own work, including R, Python, Stata, SAS, or SPSS. There are no required prerequisites. Having taken (or currently taking) an introductory statistics or research methods course is helpful, but it is not mandatory.
The skills you build here are useful far beyond the classroom and beyond academic research. You will learn how to work with large and messy real-world data, how to ask a clear question and find the answer in the numbers, how to make simple charts and tables that tell a story, and how to explain your findings to people who are not experts.
course.objectives:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
Understand how the major international surveys (WVS, EASS, ISSP, PISA, and SAGE) are built, and why they are useful for studying how people think, behave, live, and learn in different countries.
Prepare and clean real survey data, and run basic to intermediate analysis using the software of your choice.
Ask a clear research question and test it with care, while watching for common problems in comparing countries (for example, sampling, and whether a question means the same thing in each country).
Write and present your own short research that compares countries or studies a topic in an international setting.
Turn data into a clear story: make simple charts and tables, draw honest conclusions, and explain your findings to people who are not experts.

course.description:
Course Description:
The legal regime regulating the rights and obligations of States in their use of the seas has long been one of the most dynamic and important areas of International law. Various economic activities of humankind take place in the seas and oceans, and, at times, they are also hot spots for regional tensions and conflicts. The law of the sea provides the legal framework reflected in the wealth of customary laws, treaty laws, and judicial opinions dealing with this subject.
This course provides a full picture of the legal framework of the state practice in the seas, mainly the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. Emphasis will be given on the issues of state sovereignty and their sovereign rights in maritime zones, due regard when when states exercise maritime freedom and rights, mechanism of dispute settlement, and enviroment aspects regarding climate change and living resources. Law enforcement and military activities on the seas will also be equally addressed, among others.
The theories and state practice will be introduced through the rulings of international judicial bodies and academic treatises. Students will have a chance to examine the balance of rights and interests between states and between states and the international community and identify the challenges to the legal framework from emerging issues on environment protection, climate change, and maritime security.

course.objectives:
Learning Objectives and Outcomes
Objectives
Mastering Transition and Governance:
Comprehend the impacts of net-zero transitions and water scarcity on corporate operations, and master the best practices of social responsibility, regulatory compliance, and corporate governance.
Connecting Social Strategy with Performance:
Deeply explore the practical execution of social responsibility (particularly international human rights, family care, and DEI) and its long-term impact on corporate reputation, talent attraction, and financial/fiscal health.
Advanced Sustainability Report Deconstruction:
Cultivate the ability to independently read and critically analyze quantitative E, S, and G metrics and implementation timelines within the sustainability reports of tech, textile, and luxury retail sectors.
Strategic Proposal and Critical Thinking:
Develop problem-solving capabilities to combine fiscal tools and organizational strategy to formulate concrete, actionable solutions for corporate governance deficiencies and supply chain vulnerabilities.
Outcomes
Critical Evaluation of Cross-Industry Sustainability Strategies
Students will be able to independently read, deconstruct, and critically analyze the English sustainability reports of multinational corporations across tech, traditional manufacturing, and luxury retail sectors. They will develop the practical capacity to precisely evaluate actual implementation progress against environmental (E) commitments (e.g., water stewardship and net-zero targets) and effectively identify potential greenwashing practices.
Strategic Planning for Social Responsibility and Inclusive Governance
Students will be able to proficiently apply international human rights and Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) frameworks to deeply dissect the variations in employee welfare and family-care strategies across diverse industries. They will acquire the skills to formulate forward-looking strategic plans and actionable solutions for multinational organizations aiming to protect labor rights and optimize work-life balance
Audit and Assessment of Corporate Governance, Legal Compliance, and Supply Chain Management Risks:
Integrating finance and business strategy perspectives, students will be able to systematically evaluate a corporation's compliance thresholds, tax transparency performance, and the execution of its global supply chain governance. They will be equipped to accurately identify and assess potential fiscal risks and reputational damages arising from governance failures or regulatory non-compliance.
教學目標
掌握轉型與治理精髓：
理解淨零轉型與水資源壓力對企業運營的影響，並熟練掌握社會責任、合規性及公司治理的最佳實踐。
深掘社會責任與績效關聯：
深入探討社會責任（尤指國際人權、家庭照護與 DEI）的實務操作，及其對企業形象、人才吸引力與財務績效的長期影響。

培養獨立閱讀並批判性分析科技業、紡織成衣業與奢侈品零售業英文永續報告書中 E、S、G 數據與執行進度的能力。
展現策略提案與批判思考：
培養學生分析和解決問題的能力，能結合財政工具與組織策略，針對企業在供應鏈管理及合規缺陷上提出具體的建議方案。

公司治理、法律遵循合規性與供應鏈風險之審查能力

course.description:
Course Description
Contemporary society seems to be grappling with numerous crises and challenges! In 2000, United Nations member states collectively signed the Millennium Declaration, aiming to tackle major global issues such as poverty and hunger through collaborative efforts. In a similar vein, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation launched the Grand Challenges initiative in 2003, seeking to identify significant contemporary challenges and promote the development of innovative solutions. Coinciding with this, in 2008, the U.S. National Academy of Engineering announced 14 Grand Challenges for engineering, aimed at driving research to solve complex and intractable social problems, often referred to as "wicked social problems." Following this approach, the European Union in 2014 identified seven major societal challenges to guide technological development policies. Finally, in 2015, the United Nations updated the global challenges and introduced the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), outlining seventeen major challenges that the global community should overcome by 2030. It is evident that the international community increasingly relies on the concept of "Grand Challenges" to define and address the various social problems facing humanity.
As the world confronts various "Grand Challenges," there is a growing tendency to look toward potential "innovations" as solutions to these global crises. Increasing resources are being allocated to promote diverse innovations aimed at addressing these significant challenges. This reliance on technological advancements to solve major social issues is also reflected in international policy-making. In 2014, the European Union introduced the Horizon 2020 research and innovation program, with the primary objective of using "Responsible Research and Innovation" to tackle key societal challenges. Similarly, in 2015, when the United Nations unveiled the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), it also released a policy white paper detailing how science, technology, and innovation (STI) can be harnessed to achieve these goals.
Various issues arise following this trend. What are these innovations being promoted by international agencies? How could we discern whether these innovations could really solve the social and environmental problems without unintended consequences? In short, how could we develop a deeper understanding of these innovations as solutions to global problems?
These are questions that constitute the basis of this course. In this course, relying on perspectives from different disciplines in social sciences, we are going to collectively explore the landscape of innovation in the international development field. We will also learn to develop various analytical tools to assess potential and existing innovations poised to solve grand challenges.
Course Format
Class Activity & Group Discussion & Short Lecture:
I employ a
student-centered learning approach
in this course rather than a traditional lecture format (i.e., you listen to lectures to learn knowledge).
My role will be a facilitator who supports your learning. In particular, this course is built on group discussion and collective learning. Most learning will be based on reading assigned materials, discussion, and class activities. I will supplement these activities with short lectures that help contextualize readings, articulate learning themes across weeks, and move the discussion forward.
Learning Activities
Collective Annotation:
For most of the weeks, there is one assigned reading you need to finish reading before coming to the class. You will also be required to make 3 comments and reply to 3 comments on a collective reading document. Your comments will be incorporated into the classroom activity and discussion.
Class participation and end-of-class exercise
It is critical to come to the class on time and participate in class activities. My assumption is that a fair proportion of your learning will come from your interaction and collaboration with your classmates during the class. Thus, it is imperative to attend every class except for legitimate reasons (e.g. sick leave or other types of leave permitted by the university).
Case Study – Exploring Taiwan’s innovation beyond the semiconductor sector
Throughout the course, you will also need to pair with the other student and investigate a specific innovation in Taiwan beyond the semiconductor sector. At the end of the semester, each group of students will need to produce a 3000-word piece of essay. Your essay will have the chance to be included in a special issue in the
Taiwan Insight
online magazine website if it meets the standard.
To prepare each group to work on your case study, we will learn a series of analytical questions and different kinds of “stakeholder analysis” mapping tools that could allow you to carry out the analysis. You will also have the opportunity to carry out some fieldwork to study the case better.
I will also assist you to finish this essay every step of the way. There are NINE assignments throughout the semester to help you craft the essay. I will also provide a more detailed guideline for each assignment during the course. These assignments include:
Initial proposal
Fieldwork proposal
Fieldwork report
Initial description of the case
Analysis outline
In-person office-hour consultation with the instructor
First draft
Draft workshopping (W15 & W16)
Finalized article
The Innovation This Week:
To facilitate you to cultivate familiarity with innovations across the global development arena and develop tools and skills to stay connected with the global world, I developed this learning activity called “The Innovation This Week.” Everyone will rotate to share the background of one specific innovation. I will give you a more specific guideline during the class.
Study Journal:
Study Journal is a Google document you share with me. I will provide detailed instructions later for how to create your Study Journal. I hope this Study Journal will serve as a platform for you to monitor and track your learning progress. It will also be a good way for me to know how you are doing during these four months and what measures I could do to support your learning. You will be responsible for maintaining this Study Journal throughout the 4-month course. In specific, this Study Journal will include four components.
At the beginning of the course, you will need to develop your learning schedule for all the course assignments stated in the syllabus. (mandatory)
In the 9
th
week of the course, you will need to do a mid-term reflection to evaluate your learning so far and how you may adjust your study plan in the next two months. (mandatory)
At the end of the course, you will need to write a brief report evaluating your learning during these four months. (mandatory)
You are welcome to write an update on your learning progress and status any time during the semester (e.g., once a week) on the same document. (optional)
course.objectives:
Learning Outcome
During this course, you will have the opportunity to learn how to:
recognize the differences, similarities, and connections between various types of innovations.
identify and analyze the broader context of global issues underlying particular innovations.
apply multiple approaches and perspectives to assess specific innovations.
develop stakeholder analysis skills.
identify (in)effective ways of reading, writing, and participating in group discussion.

course.titleZh: 蓋婭政治與戰時生態學
course.description:
The notion of Gaia-politics challenges traditional approaches to sovereignty by taking more seriously the geo of geopolitics, that is to say its environmental dimension. War ecology is another concept that aims to address the concomitance of the climate emergency with more traditional threats on national security including military and civilian defense. Through guess lectures, off campus visits and negotiation theaters, the class focuses on the case of Taiwan in comparison with other countries.
In 2023, this course focused on conflicts between humans and non-humans. In 2024, we paid attention to the role of social movements (such as environmental protection and antinuclear mobilization), and how they connect with national politics, in particular state agencies and the parliament. In 2025, we explored with a critical eye the catchwords of ‘social resilience’, ‘technological innovation’ and ‘energy transition’, and how these effectively influence collective preparation to climate change and war scenarios.
In 2026, while continuing our research on these topics, we will also conduct an educational experiment that requires us to spend most of our time out of the classroom. The idea is to take a pause, detox from our overuse of electronics and AI, and return to the basics of ethnographic fieldwork with our eyes and ears wide open, using handwritten notes and drawings.
「蓋婭政治」(Gaia-politics)的概念挑戰了「主權」 概念的傳統取徑，因為蓋婭政治更認真看待「地緣政治」中的「地緣」，也就是其環境面向。「戰爭生態學」(war ecology)則是另一個概念，旨在面對氣候緊急狀態與傳統國安威脅(包括軍事與民間防 衛)共存的局勢。
透過客座課程、校外參訪與協商劇場的形式，本課 程將聚焦於台灣相較於其他國家的情勢。2023年， 本課程聚焦於人類與非人類之間的衝突。2024年， 我們更注重社會運動(如環保與反核運動)的角 色，以及它們如何與國內政治——特別是政府機構與國會——產生連結。
2025年，我們將在延續對跨物種正義、社會運動與 國家政治的關注之餘，進一步批判性地探討「社會 韌性」、「科技創新」與「能源轉型」這些關鍵詞，並檢視它們如何實質地影響集體面對氣候變遷與戰爭 情境的準備與應對能力。
2026年，我們除了將繼續探索上述議題，亦會將多數時間移至教室之外，進行一項教育性實驗計畫。本計畫旨在按下暫停鍵，戒斷我們對3C產品與人工智慧的過度使用；並以敏銳的觀察與傾聽，透過手寫與手繪紀錄，回歸民族誌田野工作的基礎。
course.objectives:
The goal of this mixed-method approach—using ethnographic fieldwork and negotiation theater—is to improve our capacity to detach from electronic devices and increase our focus while reading scientific papers, attending lectures, participating in group discussions, and conducting ethnographic fieldwork. In other words, this means listening and observing, taking valuable notes, and turning these observations into social capital and political will through class discussions. Meanwhile, protests against the environmental cost of electronic waste and the huge carbon footprint of AI data centers provide further reminders and incentives to detox from electronics. Last but not least, as Taiwan’s civil defense organizations train their members, we must also learn to cope with electricity shortages or blackouts in the event of a military emergency, natural hazard, or industrial disaster (such as earthquakes, typhoons, or gas explosions).
課程目標與預期成果：本課程透過民族誌田野工作與協商劇場的混合途徑，旨在幫助我們降低對電子產品的依賴，藉此提升在閱讀文獻、參與講座、小組討論與田野工作時的專注力。具體而言，我們將練習觀察與傾聽、作好筆記，並透過課堂討論將這些觀察轉化為社會資本與政治動能。此外，遠離 3C 也是對當前社會與環境議題的反思。電子垃圾的環境代價與 AI 資料中心的巨大碳足跡，不斷提醒並促使我們減少對電子設備的依賴。最後，正如台灣民防組織對其會員的訓練，我們也必須透過這門課學會：在遭遇軍事衝突或天災人禍（如地震、颱風、氣爆）時，如何面對並適應缺電或停電的狀態。

course.description:
‘Introduction to Political Science’ is a one-semester module for undergraduate students. It aims at (1) presenting the scope and core areas of political science to students, (2) nurturing their abilities to reflect on politics, and (3) developing their abilities to express their analysis and interpretation of politics through coherent arguments.
The module, therefore, is organised into two major themes: political phenomena and ideas, with a strong emphasis on the theory and history of political science. Apart from the first two weeks that introduce the theme of the module and its historical origins, the module unfolds with (1) the mapping of key political phenomena (week 3-7), before moving onto (2) the essential aspects of politics (week 9-15). To conclude the module, the last two weeks will include an open discussion on the future of political science (week 15), and a three-round debate (week 16).
course.objectives:
The objectives of the module include (1) familiarising the students with the core analytical or interpretative objects and approaches of political science, (2) cultivating the students’ ability to think critically about the political environment they find themselves in, and (3) encouraging students to form and present their political arguments in public in a debate.
The design of the assignments, including the essay abstract (mid-term), class debate (week 16), and term paper (end of term), aims to help students develop the ability to form coherent and succinct arguments and present them in an articulate, well-informed, and academically sound term essay.

course.description:
Sustainable development has been ardently advocated by numerous international institutions, governments, NGOs, and corporations in recent years. Despite its growing prominence, the concept of sustainable development is broad and complex. One illustrative example of its scope is the United Nations' 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). These cover a wide array of interconnected objectives, ranging from poverty eradication and climate action, to ensuring inclusive education and beyond.
Navigating these multifaceted and often nebulous concepts can pose a significant challenge. The tasks of defining these goals, assessing progress, and crafting effective strategies are no small feats. Yet, the advent of advanced data analysis tools and techniques provides a promising pathway to address these complex issues. Especially in the recent years, GenAI's development has offered opportunities for the analysis of sustainable issues.
course.objectives:
This course is designed to illuminate this intersection. Its goal is to equip students with the necessary knowledge and skills to apply data analysis in the context of sustainable development. Through this journey, students will cultivate a robust understanding of how to define, evaluate, and address sustainable development goals using data-driven approaches and AI agents.
This course is designed to leverage data analysis in order to evaluate the ways in which various groups and classes mobilize to promote their agendas, ultimately impacting the progress of sustainable development. These social actors encompass corporations, trade associations, social classes, racial and ethnic groups, as well as the state. Through this course, you will embark on a journey into a dynamic and rapidly evolving field that has the potential to drive significant change on corporate, national, and even global levels.

course.titleZh: 種族、宗教、民族主義：全球的暴力與歸屬政治
course.titleEn: Ethnicity, Religion, Nationalism:Violence and the Politics of Belonging in the Global World
course.description:
Notes:
Essays
: Students write
1 essay (1000 words), due at the mid-term
. This essay is written in a style of policy commentary. For this essay, students choose for themselves at least 2 theories from the 16-week course, and a case study.
Final paper
: Students write
1 individual final paper (4,000-5,000 words) due at the end of the course
. Students choose the topic of these final papers themselves.
Presentations
: Students present twice: 1 on the weekly topic of their choice, 1 very short 5-minute presentation on the framework of their final papers.
The course includes
stimulating activities such as debates, games, simulations, and watching a film. Film Title: Argo (2012), a three-Oscar-winning film about the rescue of US embassy employees from the siege of the American embassy in Tehran, Iran. Director: Ben Affleck. This film shows how Iran’s religious nationalism and US secular nationalism clashed during the 1979 Iranian revolution.
Alternatively the course is planned to introduce
an innovative learning method which includes visits to religious civil society organizations to discuss with religious leaders/activists on the interplay between “religion” and “nationalism”, the organizations are: the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan (PCT) or the Tzu-Chi Foundation.
In light of the prolonged Israeli-Hamas war and the ongoing tensions between the United States  and Iran, observers have warned of the possibility of a serious regional escalation and renewed global instability in the near future. The course “Ethnicity, Religion, Nationalism: Violence and the Politics of Belonging in the Global World” provides a structured space for students to critically examine how ethnic and religious identities shape nationalism and contribute to political conflict and violence in different regional and international contexts.
The course explores the interaction between religion and ethnic identities in Asia (East Asia, South Asia and Southeast Asia), the Middle East, and the United States, and their impact on the construction of nationalism. It addresses critical questions of identity and citizenship, inclusion and exclusion, emotional and symbolic attachments, and the linkage between local and global political dynamics. The course asks how ethnicity and religion shape political interaction, how ethnic and religious identities may aggravate conflict or strengthen cooperation, and how they are mobilized in processes of nation-building and political legitimation. It further examines how relevant dimensions such as sacralization and symbolic forms of legitimation may lead to conflict and violence.
The course is divided into two parts. The first part introduces key concepts of ethnicity, religion, identity, nation, and nationalism, and examines major theoretical explanations for the emergence and persistence of nationalism. The second part focuses on the political consequences of nationalism for belonging and identity, including religious nationalism, fundamentalism, and identity-based conflict, through case studies from China, Myanmar, Thailand, Indonesia, India, Turkey, Israel, and the United States.
The course also considers the role of digital technologies and artificial intelligence in shaping contemporary identity politics and nationalist mobilisation. Social media platforms, algorithmic systems, and AI-generated content increasingly mediate the circulation of ethnic and religious narratives, often amplifying polarization and reshaping boundaries of inclusion and exclusion in the process.
On Week 12 students will watch the film “Argo” (2012, Director: Ben Affleck)
,
an Oscar-winning film which depicts the 1979 rescue of six U.S. State Department employees during the siege at the American embassy in Tehran, Iran.
Alternatively, the
course will include an
Innovative Learning Method Week with Study Visits to religious organizations
. Planned visits include the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan (PCT), or Tzu-Chi Foundation, where students will engage with
religious leaders and practitioners to discuss the interplay between “religion” and “nationalism”, and conflict.
course.objectives:
After completing the course, students will:
Understand the meaning of key concepts, such as ethnicity, religion, identity, nation, nationalism, religious nationalism and fundamentalism.
Understand the interaction and complex relations between these key concepts and their role in the politics of belonging and citizenship in various countries.
Understand the interaction and complex relations between these key concepts and their role in fundamentalism and/or political violence in various countries.
Be able to analyze current and/or past conflicts by examining how ethnicity and religion generate nationalism, which in turn may produce violence and political conflict in the global world.
Be able to critically assess how digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) shape the circulation, amplification, and contestation of ethnic, religious, and nationalist narratives, and how these processes influence contemporary forms of identity politics and conflict.

course.description:
International organisations (IOs) have been created over the past century to advance cooperation among states to find common solutions to international and transnational challenges. IOs are tools of international politics and international relations, while serving as indispensable fora for establishing and implementing international norms and principles. Some of the key international challenges tackled by IOs include armed conflicts, humanitarian crises, infectious diseases, climate change, international trade and global inequality. IOs vary greatly in terms of their mission, functions, membership, structure, powers and geographical scope. The role of IOs in international politics remains controversial: while some perceive them as enablers to achieving global solutions beyond the capacity of individual states, others question their effectiveness and legitimacy given their tendency to be controlled by the most powerful states. States and citizens alike are sometimes disappointed by the gap between IOs’ lofty aspirations and their actual performance in addressing global problems.
The course will start by introducing the central analytical approaches that help students understand key characteristics of international organisations: their creation and design, their power and mandates, their decision-making processes, their impact and policy effectiveness, and their interaction with states and other IOs. This analytical framework is then applied to analyse the functions and performance of IOs concerning specific global challenges and policy domains, including peace, security, human rights, trade, crisis response, health and environment. Finally, the course will examine the responsibility and accountability of IOs, and examine the geopolitical realities that limit Taiwan’s participation in these international fora.
The course will be taught by Associate Professor Kevin Chang (JD, LLM, MA, GradDipIntLaw, GradDipLegPrac, BSc), who is a senior advisor on international law and who brings more than 20 years’ experience as a lawyer, advocate and practitioner with the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the Australian Government and other international organisations. Professor Chang is a Lawyer of the Supreme Court of the Australian Capital Territory. He also teaches at the University of Sydney and the Graduate Institute of International and Development Studies in Geneva.
This course will be taught via a hybrid mode of teaching of 50% being in-person, the other 50% online. Students are expected to read the prescribed reading material in advance, submit reflection notes, and participate in class discussions. This course is designed with an assumption that students will already have a solid appreciation of international politics. This course is suitable only for students who have an advanced level of English proficiency. Because of the class size limit of 25 students, prospective students may be required to submit a statement of motivation prior to their enrolment being confirmed.
course.objectives: The key aim of this course is to gain a deep understanding of IOs and their capacities for solving the world’s greatest challenges. Students will gain detailed knowledge of IOs through analysis of their characteristics, powers, legitimacy and performance, and will recognise the promises and limitations of IOs in the modern global system. Students will understand the powers possessed by IOs, as well as challenges faced by them, through examining their performance with respect to major global issues and crises.

course.titleEn: Hybrid Regimes: Democratic Challenges in Southeast Asia
course.description:
Notes:
Essays
: Students write
1 essay (1000 words), due at the mid-term
. This essay is written in a style of policy commentary. For this essay, students choose for themselves at least 2 theories from the 16-week course, and a case study.
The best essays will be chosen for publication submission at prominent policy platforms of Southeast Asia politics, such as ISEAS’ Fulcrum in Singapore or East Asia Forum in Australia, after sufficient editing.
Final paper
: Students write
1 individual final paper (4,000-5,000 words) due at the end of the course
. Students choose the topic for these final papers themselves.
Presentations
: Students present twice:
1 on the weekly topic of their choice, and 1 (very short, 5-minute presentation) on the framework of their final papers.
The course includes stimulating activities such as debates, games, simulations, and discussing a film
. Two alternatives: (1) “
The Kingmaker” (2019) an award-winning documentary film portraying the political career of Imelda Marcos of the Philippines
, the widow of the former president of the Philippines, with a focus on the efforts to rehabilitate the family's image and to return to political power (2)
“I Not Stupid” (
小孩不笨
)
(2002), an award-winning Singaporean political satire comedy about the lives, struggles and adventures of three elementary school students
. The film sparked public discussions and parliamentary debates that led to real reforms in the education system.
The course is also tentatively planned to include an innovative learning method called “Learning Together”: in one of the weeks, our students will be learning together with students from NTNU’s Department of East Asia Studies. This will be done either by receiving NTNU’s students in our classroom or by visiting NTNU’s class on politics in Southeast Asia.
The course “Hybrid Regimes: Democratic Challenges in Southeast Asia” is designed as a standalone course or as a follow-up course for students who have completed the introductory course “Politics in Southeast Asia: Change and Continuity”. The course examines the socio-political development of authoritarian and hybrid regimes in Asia, enabling students to survey, compare, and analyze the persistent challenges of democratization in the region. While the empirical focus is Southeast Asia, the course also situates regional political dynamics within broader geopolitical relations, particularly with East Asian actors such as China, Taiwan, and Japan. Cambodia’s limited democratization, for instance, has been analyzed by some scholars in relation to its close ties with China. From this perspective, democratization in Southeast Asia may also be influenced by engagement with consolidated democracies, such as Taiwan and Japan.
The course further engages with Taiwan’s foreign policy initiative, the NEW SOUTHBOUND POLICY, through which Taiwan seeks to deepen economic, political, and cultural relations with Southeast Asian countries.
In the aftermath of the Cold War, a global wave of democratization reshaped political systems across Asia, Central and Eastern Europe, Latin America, and Sub-Saharan Africa. The dissolution of the Soviet Union weakened the legitimacy of many authoritarian regimes, leading to transitions toward multiparty systems and liberal reforms. However, regime transitions did not always result in democratic consolidation, and many states experienced stalled or reversed democratization processes.
While pure authoritarian regimes have become less common in Asia, many states are better understood as “hybrid regimes” or “electoral autocracies”, positioned between liberal democracy and authoritarian rule. These regimes typically maintain the formal structures of electoral competition, including multiparty elections, while systematically limiting opposition voices through institutional manipulation, uneven political competition, and selective enforcement of rules. In these nations, the thin veneer of quasi-democratic institutions and multi-party elections became a façade for abuses of power, manipulation and corruption. In Thailand, following the 2019 election, the military-backed government dissolved an opposition party and arrested activists, triggering widespread student-led protests demanding constitutional reform and greater civil liberties. In 2023, although the opposition Move Forward Party won the election, it was prevented from forming a government due to institutional constraints and entrenched political interests. In the Philippines in 2016, voter dissatisfaction with crime and entrenched elite politics contributed to the election of Rodrigo Duterte, whose administration was associated with an extensive “war on drugs” involving extrajudicial killings. In 2022, voters elected Ferdinand Marcos Jr., the son and namesake of the former dictator, signaling the persistence of dynastic politics. In Myanmar, the military coup in 2021 marked a reversal of electoral democratization and a return to direct military rule.
The course also incorporates analysis of the role of digital technologies in shaping political competition and state-society relations in Southeast Asia
.
Social media platforms have become central arenas for electoral mobilization, political communication, and contestation in hybrid regimes.
Emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), further amplify these dynamics by enabling new forms of political communication and information manipulation at scale.
In several cases, coordinated online networks, including troll activities and disinformation campaigns, were deployed during election periods to influence public opinion and delegitimize opposition actors. Concurrently,
states have introduced regulatory frameworks such as anti-fake news legislation and cybersecurity laws, which, while formally justified in terms of public order and information integrity, may also function as instruments of digital surveillance
and constraints on freedom of expression. These developments underscore how hybrid regimes are sustained not only through formal institutions and coercive mechanisms, but also through digital infrastructures and information environments.
Some of the questions the course seeks to answer are: What is democracy good for? Why do some states democratize while others continue to exhibit authoritarianism? How do highly corrupt political regimes survive for decades? How do populist leaders gain and maintain power in Asia? What is the legacy of political violence in newly democratic states? What is the legacy of military rule in the region? How do global human rights values and “Asian values” shape political development in the region? How do digital technologies, including social media platforms, disinformation networks, and state regulatory frameworks, reshape political competition, state-society relations, and the boundaries of free expression in hybrid regimes? The course begins by introducing core concepts, regime typologies, and indicators for assessing democratization. It subsequently examines in-depth developments in Thailand, the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Myanmar, Vietnam, and Cambodia.

course.description:
International trade is the economic backbone of most countries in the world. The development of information technologies has pushed forward the trade facilitation and digitalization of cross border exchange. The digital transformation of international trade has reduced the operation time and costs, facilitated the global value chain, and connected the trade and logistics communities globally.
Cross border digital trade attracts higher attention than ever in the post COVID-19 era. While normal international trade procedures and operations which are heavily dependent on paper-documents are interrupted, the use of technologies helps to make the international trade more resilient and lower the barriers of physical documentation. International initiatives as well as respective government’s actions in the implementation of cross border digital trade to increase the scale, scope and speed of trade will be introduced in this course. Challenges including the adoption of new technologies, policy and regulation issues, change of user behavior during the implementation of cross border digital trade will also be discussed in the course.
This course aims to develop students’ knowledge about the digitalization of international trade for increasing their competitive edges in the global business setting.

To enable students with knowledge of cross border digital trade

course.description:
本課程以頭前溪流域為學習場域，結合永續發展目標（SDGs）、環境治理與設計思考方法，帶領學生從真實世界問題出發，探討
河川生態、水質污染、水資源治理、環境正義及地方文化等議題。課程透過課堂講授、實地走讀、專家座談、資料分析與團隊

會與治理面向之創新方案，並藉由與在地社群、學校及公民團體互動，深化對流域治理與公共參與的理解，培養面對永續發展

course.objectives: Course keywords: 永續環境治理 Sustainable Environmental Governance,設計思考 Design Thinking,流域治理 Watershed Governance,水資源管理 Water Resource Management,社會實踐與公民參與 Social Practice and Civic Engagement      永續環境治理的設計思考Design Thinking for Sustainable Environmental Governance: Living in Harmony with the Hsinchu River一、課程說明（Course Description）頭前溪是孕育新竹地區發展的重要流域，也是新竹縣市民生用水、生態環境與產業發展的重要基礎。本課程以頭前溪流域為學習場域，結合永續發展目標（SDGs）、環境治理、設計思考（Design Thinking）及大學社會責任（USR）理念，引導學生從真實世界問題出發，探討河川生態、水質污染、水資源管理、環境正義、公民參與及地方文化等議題。課程透過課堂講授、跨域討論、專家座談、實地踏查、資料分析與團隊專題等方式，培養學生問題分析、利害關係人溝通、跨域整合及方案設計能力。學生將運用設計思考流程，從問題同理、需求探索、問題定義、方案發想、原型設計到成果驗證，提出兼顧環境、社會與治理面向之創新方案。本課程特別強調「從流域認識地方、從地方理解永續」，鼓勵學生走入頭前溪流域現場，透過與地方社群、學校、公民團體及政府部門互動，理解環境治理的複雜性與多元利害關係人觀點，培養未來面對永續發展挑戰所需之專業能力與社會責任感。---二、指定用書（Text Books）教師自編講義、案例教材及補充閱讀資料。---三、參考書籍（References）1. Brown, T. (2009). *Change by Design: How Design Thinking Creates New Alternatives for Business and Society.*2. United Nations. *Transforming Our World: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.*3. United Nations World Water Development Report.4. EPA (United States Environmental Protection Agency) Water Resources and Public Participation Resources.5. Climate Change Impacts on Freshwater Resources, EPA.6. Kernan, M., Battarbee, R., & Moss, B. (2010). *Climate Change Impacts on Freshwater Ecosystems.*7. 台灣河溪網（Taiwan River Network）8. 荒野保護協會（Society of Wilderness）9. 我們要喝乾淨水行動聯盟10. 頭前溪流域相關研究報告、政府公開資料及教師指定閱讀。---#四、教學方式（Teaching Methods）本課程採取「問題導向學習（PBL）」與「場域導向學習（Place-based Learning）」方式進行。教學方式包含：1. 課堂講授（Lectures）   * 永續發展、流域治理、水資源管理及設計思考相關理論。2. 分組討論（Group Discussion）   * 問題分析、需求探索及方案發想。3. 實地踏查（Field Study）   * 頭前溪流域、水環境場域及相關設施參訪。4. 專家座談（Guest Speakers）   * 邀請學界、政府、NGO及實務工作者分享經驗。5. 專題實作（Project-based Learning）   * 學生團隊提出永續環境治理方案。6. 成果展示（Presentation）   * 期中與期末成果發表與交流。---五、教學進度（Course Schedule）Week 1　課程介紹與頭前溪流域概論Week 2-3　實地走讀：舊港島、南寮及頭前溪出海口（9/19全天）Week 4　頭前溪流域地理、水文與歷史發展Week 5　河川生態、水質污染與環境風險Week 6　專家講座：河川廢棄物與公民科學Week 7　流域實地考察與現場觀察Week 8　頭前溪與新竹城市發展Week 9　期中成果報告Week 10　永續治理案例與利害關係人參與Week 11　公私協力與水環境巡守實務Week 12　關西鳳山溪走讀Week 13　竹東流域文化與地方走讀Week 14　垃圾處理與循環經濟場域參訪Week 15　水質大數據分析與治理應用Week 16　期末成果發表與方案展示---六、成績考核（Evaluation）課堂參與與出席　　　　　20%（含課堂討論、活動參與）團隊合作與平時作業　　　30%期中專題成果　　　　　　20%期末專題成果　　　　　　30%學生請假規定依《國立清華大學學生請假辦法》辦理。本課程包含多次實地踏查及場域學習活動，若因特殊原因無法參與校外教學活動，須依學校規定完成請假程序，並於事前通知授課教師。經核准請假者，應依教師指定方式完成替代學習作業，以維護學習權益。無故缺席校外活動者，將視同缺課並影響課堂參與成績。---七、生成式AI使用規範（AI Usage Policy）■ 有條件開放（Conditionally Open）本課程鼓勵學生善用生成式AI工具（如ChatGPT、Claude、Gemini等）作為學習輔助工具，例如資料蒐集、文獻摘要、構想發想、簡報整理及文本潤飾等。惟學生須遵守以下原則：1. AI不得取代學生之獨立思考與分析。2. 專題報告與作業須明確說明AI工具使用情形。3. 學生需自行查證AI產出內容之正確性。4. 實地觀察、田野調查、數據分析與個人反思不得完全由AI代為完成。5. 教師得要求學生說明作品形成過程及AI使用方式。未依規定揭露AI使用情形者，得視情況調整成績評定。---八、課程相關網站（Course-related Website）1. 聯合國永續發展目標（SDGs）   https://sdgs.un.org/goals2. 台灣河溪網   https://www.twrna.org3. 荒野保護協會   https://www.sow.org.tw4. 我們要喝乾淨水行動聯盟   https://www.facebook.com/hsinchu.drink5. 頭前溪流域行動平台（課程期間提供）

course.description:
This course is designed to provide a basic understanding of surface analysis techniques and the 
applications how surface analysis can be utilized in research. In addition to conventional 
characterization, advanced experimental design for surface analysis, such as synchrotron-based 
techniques, in situ methodologies and time-resolved experiments, are also introduced in this course.

course.description:
本課程介紹質譜技術於環境分析之原理與應用，涵蓋液相與氣相層析串聯質譜（LC–MS/MS、GC–MS/MS）及感應耦合電漿質譜
（ICP–MS），並說明不同類型污染物之分析策略。課程強調環境污染物之檢測原理與應用，培養學生於環境監測與污染分析之基
本能力。
course.objectives: Course keywords: 環境質譜分析、新興污染物、層析分離技術、微量分析、環境監測 Environmental Mass Spectrometry、Emerging Contaminants、Chromatographic Separation、Trace Analysis、Environmental Monitoring      一、課程說明(Course Description)本課程旨在建立學生對質譜技術於環境分析中之核心概念與應用能力，內容涵蓋層析分離（液相與氣相液相）與質譜分析之整合，並結合LC–MS/MS、GC–MS/MS及ICP–MS等主流分析平台。課程將說明不同污染物之分析方法與儀器選擇原則，並介紹樣品前處理、定量分析、品質控制及數據判讀等關鍵技術。此外，亦將涵蓋新興污染物分析、非目標篩選及轉化產物鑑定等進階主題，修課學生將具備跨領域之環境分析能力，並能將質譜技術應用於實際研究問題。二、指定用書(Text Books)“Introduction to MassSpectrometry” J.T. Watson and O.D.Sparkman, 4th Edition, Wiley.“Mass Spectrometry-Principles andApplications” Edmond de Hoffmannand Vincent Stroobant, 3rd Edition,Wiley三、參考書籍(References)四、教學方式(Teaching Method)Lecture五、教學進度(Syllabus)LC–MS/MS、GC–MS/MS、ICP–MS六、成績考核(Evaluation)1.Midterm: 40%2.Final exam: 40%3.Report: 20%七、可連結之網頁位址

course.description:
This course introduces students to the core concepts and methods of statistics, with a
focus on learning how to use data effectively in the face of uncertainty. Key topics
include data visualization, descriptive statistics, probability, statistical inference, and
linear regression. Emphasis will be placed on building intuition and practical
understanding rather than mathematical rigor.
Students will develop the skills to make sense of data, draw meaningful conclusions,
and communicate results with clarity and confidence. The tools and thinking
developed in this course are valuable for making informed decisions and conducting
research across a wide range of disciplines. They also form the foundation of many
modern applications, including machine learning and artificial intelligence.

course.description:
本門課程設計從基礎的程式設計開始，透過循序漸進的修課規劃，讓學生除有完備的人工智慧技術外，也了解相關倫理議

值。

course.description:

are contextualized. Students will explore how modern AI models are integrated into real-world
systems such as robots, smart homes, and autonomous vehicles, and how intelligence,
embodiment, and environment jointly shape system behavior.
As AI systems increasingly operate around us in everyday life, critical questions emerge: How
do these systems function in real-world settings? How do we ensure their reliability, safety, and
alignment with human values? And what new challenges arise when AI is deployed in open,
dynamic environments?
If these questions inspire you, this course is designed for you.

course.description:
自二十世紀初現代考古學從西方傳入中國，這門學問便很快地在歷史悠久、族群及文化多元的中國土地上生根成長，至今已取
得了大量的研究資料和豐富的研究成果，不只對促進中國古代人類文化和歷史研究及文明進程的新理解有重要的貢獻，即使對
其它人文、社會科學，甚而自然科學領域的一些研究課題，例如:中國古代的社會型態、經濟變遷、工藝美術、科技發展、宗
教禮制、民族發展、族群遺傳、農業起源和天文星象等，也提供了非常珍貴的出土資料與證據。有些考古發現甚而成為令人嚮
往的世界文化遺產。因此，過去半個多世紀以來的這段時間，考古學在中國成為一門顯學，被稱為是中國考古學的黃金時代。
	本課程的目的是要介紹中國考古學的發展、發現，以及重要的研究成果和所探討的重要課題，期使選課的同學對中
國考古學有所認識和瞭解，並培養研究的視野、興趣和發展的能力。

典文獻與相關主題的文本研讀，介紹人類學研究身體的相關理論、概念與研究成果，培養學生對於身體研究的興趣，理解身體與

course.description:
This seminar examines the relationships between the indigenous peoples and the  
state in Taiwan through historical periods, situating it in the settler colonial contexts.  
Historical reflection on the changing relationship between the indigenous peoples  
and the state equipped students to explain the contemporary dilemma faced by the 
indigenous people worldwide. With the concept of transitional justice emerging in  
Taiwan and elsewhere, this seminar will draw on materials and experiences in other  
Fourth World to compare with those of Taiwan’s indigenous peoples and seek to  
advance a better path forward.

course.description:
在日常生活中，許多時候情緒與倫理幾乎無法分開，而這份交纏並不止於私人生活，在現代制度之中同樣運作。本課程便從這份交纏出發，
借助人類學中兩個重要卻長期平行發展的理論傳統來理解它：倫理轉向（ethical turn）與情緒人類學（anthropology of 
emotions）。前者問的是人們如何在日常生活中成為倫理主體，後者則把情緒當作一個可以被田野觀察與描述的問題，去看人們如何在語
言、身體與人際關係之中感受、命名並賦予情緒意義。情緒的養成與倫理主體的形成，何以在許多時候難以分開，正是這門課想要一路追問
的問題。

course.description:
本課程將引導學生系統性認識考古學中石器研究的核心理論與分析方法，透過討論與案例分析，理解石器在重建人類行為與社會組織中的關
鍵角色。石器作為考古遺存中最常見且保存良好的材料之一，不僅提供了理解史前技術與日常實踐的證據，更是連結環境、經濟與文化行為
的重要媒介。課程內容涵蓋石器的類型特徵、原料選擇與取得策略、製作技術與操作序列、分類原則等基礎，以及技術組織理論、功能研
究、實驗考古學、民族考古學、過程與後過程等分析取徑，也討論如何從石器探討生計活動、勞動分工、資源利用與貿易交換等議題。透過

course.description:
This course is an undergraduate-level introduction to physical cosmology: the application of 
basic physics concepts to study the origin and evolution of the Universe. The emphasis will be on the 
"big picture" of how we learn about the structure and evolution of the universe from astronomical 
observations.
course.objectives: Course keywords: Cosmology, Astronomy, Astrophysics, Cosmological Observations, Galaxy Formation      課程說明 (Course Description)This course is an undergraduate-level introduction to the principles of cosmology: the study of the origin and evolution of the universe based on fundamental physics. The emphasis will be on astronomical observations, rather than particle physics. We will not use any mathematics more difficult than basic calculus. Although we will discuss concepts related to General Relativity, we will not do any GR calculations or derivations. The same is true for particle physics/quantum mechanics. There are no hard prerequisites for the course. However, you are expected to have a sound grasp of fundamental undergraduate physics at the 2nd-year level or above. You should understand the fundamental concepts of Newtonian gravity, special relativity and electromagnetic radiation (i.e. electron energy levels, the absorption and emission of photons) at the level of undergraduate "General Physics". Previous courses in basic astronomy will be extremely helpful.The course will be taught entirely in English, but you will be assessed on your understanding of the physical concepts, not your English ability. There will be a Mandarin-speaking TA.教學進度 (Syllabus)By the end of the course you should be able to:- Describe the principles of how distances to astronomical objects (like galaxies) are determined;- Describe the fundamental observational evidence for the expansion of the universe;- Understand the theoretical connection between the expansion of the universe and its contents;- Work with simple mathematic models of the expansion and understand how those models can be tested by observations;- Explain the origin and importance of the cosmic microwave background;- Describe the processes thought to have occurred in the first few minutes of the Universe, including "nucleosynthesis";- Explain the concepts of dark matter, dark energy and cosmic inflation;- Tell the (qualitative) story of how cosmic structures like stars and galaxies formed;- Appreciate some important open questions in modern cosmology.This course can be considered as a primer for the graduate course in cosmology offered by the Institute of Astronomy. This undergraduate course will not cover the practical, quantitative  mathematical framework needed to describe the formation and evolution of  structure, and to match cosmological observations to models. Frontier topics in cosmology will be covered only in a descriptive way, without calculations. 成績考核 (Evaluation)The exact evaluation method may be adapted depending on the class size, but will involve several homework assignments and a final exam.AI Policy: "有條件開放"Summary: AI use is acceptable as a supplement to learning, but answers to assessments must be your own work, and will be marked down for clear and uncritical use of AI tools. Use of AI in written assessments is discouraged and any such use must be clearly declared. Expect to be challenged to explain and prove your understanding if you hand in work suspected of being generated by AI without critical thought.Details: Using generative AI to help with your study is at least not worse than asking your classmates or reading random websites. There is no problem  with talking to your classmates (or AI) about the lectures or homework  assignments. You should not just accept what you are told, but always do your best to "absorb" and double-check any information on your own, and make sure you have a good "grip" on the ideas. Once you've learned about something from an AI chatbot, you should at  least try getting it to ask you some questions to test your understanding.This course involves some written assessment. Your answers to assessment  questions should *always* be your own, because the whole point of assessment is is to demonstrate to the instructor what *you* understand. Your answers to assessment questions should not come from your classmates, so they should not come from AI either. Some students use AI to "help with English". This course is not an English test, so there is absolutely no need to do that. The official language of the course is "broken English".  Your own honest answer in poor English is much better than someone else's answer in perfectly written English.教學方式 (Teaching Method)The course will be taught in a classical way, with weekly in-person lectures and recommendations for self-study. Basic lecture notes will be provided, but you are expected to read one or more textbooks by yourself.參考書籍 (References)The primary textbook for the course will be:- Introduction to Cosmology, by Barbara Ryden, 2nd Edition (Cambridge University Press, 2016) https://doi.org/10.1017/9781316651087As a second (easier but less complete) textbook, I recommend:- An Introduction to Modern Cosmology, by Andrew Liddle (3rd/revised edition, Wiley, 2015)You may also consider:- A Course in Cosmology, from Theory to Practice, by Dragan Huterer, 1st Edition (Cambridge University Press, 2023) https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009070232This is basically a slightly more advanced and up-to-date version of Ryden.More references will be given at the start of the course.

course.description:
This course is a graduate-level introduction to theories and observations of galaxy formation and 
evolution, in the concordance Dark Energy and Cold Dark Matter (LambdaCDM) cosmogony. It is a core 
course of the Institute for Astronomy graduate syllabus.
course.objectives: Course keywords: Astronomy, Astrophysics, Galaxy Observations, Galaxy Formation, Galaxy Evolution      課程說明 (Course Description)This course is a graduate-level introduction to the nature of galaxies -- what they are, where they come from, and how they change over time. These are major topics in astronomical research, building on knowledge from other areas such as cosmology and stellar astrophysics.The course is intended as a primer for graduate research. We will aim to cover a broad range of topics, rather than a rigorous mathematical treatment.PLEASE NOTE: The level will be suitable for graduate and senior undergraduate students whose major is Physics or Astrophysics. The course will assume an undergraduate background knowledge of astronomy.The course will be offered and assessed in English.The homework exercises will involve simple numerical equation-solving and graph-plotting tasks. Basic instruction in python will be provided.Students who have not previously taken a course in cosmology may find it helpful to follow the undergraduate "Introduction to Modern Cosmology" given by the same lecturer, although we will not consider more than the "big picture" of cosmology in this course.教學進度(Syllabus)The minimum syllabus is:1. Astronomical measurements and observational techniques2. Stars and stellar populations3. Describing the different types of galaxies4. The cosmological context of galaxy formation5. Galaxy "environments"6. Dark matter halo origins and structure7. The origin of galaxies, gas cooling8. Cold gas disks and star formation9. "Feedback" and chemical enrichment10. Gravitational dynamics11. Galaxy interactions and mergers12. Galaxy evolution over cosmic time13. Supermassive black holes14. Open problems in galaxy formation This course will be deliberately "simple" in assuming almost no prior knowledge.For the first time, there will be a second course in the Spring semester covering more advanced topics and details required for modern galaxy evolution research. Effectively they will be "part 1" and "part 2" of the same syllabus. The "part 2" advanced course will assume familiarity with all the topics covered here.教學方式 (Teaching Method)Lectures, reading assignments.成績考核 (Evaluation)Approximately 4 homework exercises and final quiz-style exam.指定用書 (Text Books)The reference textbook for this course will be:* "Dynamics and Astrophysics of Galaxies" by Jo Bovy (Princeton U. Press, 2026)https://galaxiesbook.org/We will not go through everything in this book, and we will not follow the chapters in the order they are presented (we will focus mostly on chapter 18).We will also make use of the classic textbook:* “An Introduction to Modern Astrophysics” (2nd ed.) by B. W. Carroll & D. A. Ostlie (2006, Pearson Addison-Wesley)Some alternative/additional textbooks about galaxies:* (Simple) Fundamentals of Galaxy Dynamics, Formation and Evolution by Ignacio Ferreras (2019, UCL Press). Free e-book: https://www.uclpress.co.uk/products/84078* (Advanced) “Galaxy Formation and Evolution” by H. Mo, S. White & F. van den Bosch(2010, Cambridge University Press)* (Advanced) “Galactic Astronomy” (2nd ed.) by J. Binney & M. Merrifield (2008, Princeton  University Press)For the cosmological background to the course, the following textbooks may be helpful:* “Introduction to Cosmology” (2nd Ed.) by Barbara Ryden (2016, Cambridge University Press)* “An Introduction to Modern Cosmology” (3rd Ed.) by Andrew Liddle  (2015, Wiley)

However, in the field of astronomy alone, nearly 40 new papers are published every day. It is a significant amount of work to keep up with this flood of papers. The purpose of this course is to train students to efficiently read and understand the essence of new research papers within a limited amount of time. Students will spend no more than one hour reading a paper of their choice and will then take turns presenting a short  summary in 10 minutes. The focus will be on understanding the main points rather than getting into the details. It is not necessary to read every single detail of the paper. Additionally, other students in the class will have a valuable opportunity to learn about the latest papers while listening to the speaker. After each presentation, the instructor will teach a relevant physics concept related to the reviewed paper.The course will take place every Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday from 12:10 pm to 1 pm. During each session, three papers will be reviewed. Therefore, over the course of one semester, we will review almost 100 papers. By the end of the semester, students will be familiar with the latest advancements in astronomy.Previous knowledge is not required. We will focus on learning key concepts of astronomy as they arise in research papers. This bottom-up approach reflects the practical and realistic nature of everyday research life. The course will be conducted in English.Use of AI : Unrestricted use with no disclosure required-參考書籍 (References)Papers to be presented are selected from the following archive servers.https://www.benty-fields.com/http://arxiv.org/list/astro-ph/new-教學方式(Teaching Method)Presentations by students followed by a review by the instructor.-成績考核(Evaluation)Presentations.-Classroom Etiquette:To create a focused learning environment, please silence your cell phones during class sessions and exams.-Presentation Policy:If you are unable to attend your scheduled presentation date, please find someone to replace well in advance. which are changing how scientific software is written, tested, and maintained. This graduate course 
teaches AI-assisted coding as a practical methodology and applies it directly to core problems in 
computational astrophysics.

LLMs operate to use them deliberately rather than superstitiously. Second, and primarily, students 
will apply AI-assisted workflows to develop, debug, and validate real astrophysical codes, from a 
simple orbit integrator up to a fluid solver and a machine-learning project.
